Network Systems Reference Guide.content:
| Reference | Use in this course |
| --- | --- |
| [IPv6 addressing, RFC 4291](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4291) | Distinguish address type, scope and interface context in Unit 2 and Unit 8. |
| [Documentation IPv4 ranges, RFC 5737](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5737) | Recognize constructed address examples in the supplied cases. |
| [HTTP semantics, RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110) | Interpret method, status, response headers and HEAD behavior in Unit 11. |
| [TLS 1.3, RFC 8446](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446) | Separate secure transport from HTTP and from the selected application identity. |
| [Linux network namespaces](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/network_namespaces.7.html) | Explain why addresses, routes, sockets and policy observations belong to a particular lab context. |

The imported README specifies each fixture's inputs, required tools and cleanup. Command syntax comes from the installed tool's manual; protocol semantics come from the relevant standard. Keep the actual command and version beside a citation when comparing results.

Network Systems Core Skills.content:
A service diagnosis follows a chain: execution context, destination lookup, selected route, next hop where needed, listening socket, policy, transport exchange and application response. A later successful observation supports only the path it actually used.

For example, an HTTP reply from `127.0.0.1:8080` proves an exchange in the issuing host's loopback context. It supplies no measurement from another machine. A listener at that same address explains why a request to the host's separate LAN address can fail. Record the bind address and issuing context before proposing a policy change.

A complete diagnosis names the first failed or unmeasured boundary, cites the exact observation, and proposes one authorized observation that could disprove the explanation.

Network Systems Next Topics.content:
The optional expansion archive introduces VPN paths, BGP reachability, wireless links and cloud policy. Each adds a boundary to the same evidence chain. A tunnel has an outer transport and an inner path; a cloud service can have both host policy and provider policy. A successful local proxy test establishes neither boundary.

Choose one topic after the capstone and draw the added boundary. Label available observations and the observation that would require a separately owned environment. A production routing deployment, public server launch or penetration test needs a separate scope and prerequisite path. This course's recorded fixture does not measure those systems.

Network Systems Boundaries.content:
Network Systems follows Linux Systems. It uses shell commands, configuration files and small supplied programs to investigate reachability and explain changes. Python and Bash source is available for inspection; the core work is networking interpretation and notebook evidence. Implementing the optional analysis functions adds programming practice.

Live ordinary-account labs use owned loopback services. Privileged routing, firewall and capture labs use their isolated Linux fixture in an owned disposable environment. The [supplied cases](/course-assets/network/network-systems-practice-pack.md) and [recorded capstone observations](/course-assets/network/recorded-capstone-observations-v1.md) support the reasoning route without a live lab. Label which route supplied the evidence.

Network Systems Prerequisite Check.content:
Before a live lab, use a Linux terminal to identify the current directory with `pwd`, list its files with `ls` and read the selected `README.md`. Know how to edit a text file, distinguish an ordinary account from root, and stop a foreground process with Control-C. Linux Systems provides the prerequisite practice.

For this supplied check, suppose the editor runs on macOS while the terminal reports `uname -s` as `Darwin`. Does opening a Linux script in the editor change where commands execute? Explain before comparing: the terminal still executes in macOS. Open the owned Linux environment's terminal for the live Linux task, or use the supplied-case route. A missing command is a setup observation, not a network diagnosis.

Network Systems Follow-Up Path.content:
After completing the capstone, choose an extension by the unanswered boundary in the runbook. For a remote-client question, study a separately scoped multi-host lab. For encrypted application behavior, study certificate deployment and application authentication after the HTTP/TLS units. For internet route selection, study routing policy after the routing and optional BGP reading.

A useful proposal names the new target environment, prerequisite, expected observation and recovery path. Example: “Compare an inner tunnel route and its outer transport in two owned VMs.” The existing loopback or namespace packet remains background evidence; new environment claims require their own observations.

Each project offers separate starter and reference roles. Both include a shared README and all listed role files. Keep those files together when exporting and extracting the ZIP. The README names the external Linux command; the browser workspace edits and saves the files.

The core notebook opens the matching saved core attempt. A transfer, extension or practice project creates a distinct attempt even when it uses the same apparatus. Network Systems Module Alignment Guide.content:
An observation, interpretation and changed case answer different questions. In the transport unit, received hexadecimal bytes are observations; identifying a missing newline as incomplete application framing is interpretation; repeating with the newline changes one condition.

Keep three notebook lines for that example: predicted boundary, actual bytes/EOF or truncation flag, and the resulting application claim. A stream ending after six payload bytes can still leave a newline-delimited message incomplete. A valid empty UDP datagram is a received message, while TCP EOF means the stream ended. Use the source's exact recorded values rather than an assumed number of receive calls.

Network Systems Reference Map.content:
Use three kinds of evidence together. A protocol reference defines meaning, an installed manual defines command options, and a saved run records what happened in one context. They answer different questions.

For an HTTP `404`, RFC 9110 explains the response semantics; the fixture README identifies the owned endpoint and request; the saved command and response show the actual exchange. For a refused TCP connection there is no HTTP status to interpret. Record the exit code and error separately. A tool's displayed `000` in that situation is not an HTTP response from the service.

Network Systems Prerequisite Map.content:
A selected route uses a destination address, so compare DNS or literal input before reasoning about that route. A socket has a transport, address and port, so read those fields before attributing a connection failure to policy. An HTTP response requires an application exchange, so distinguish it from TCP handshake evidence.

Apply the sequence to this supplied case: DNS returns `192.0.2.10`; the service listens only on `127.0.0.1:8080`; a request to the returned address is refused. The observed mismatch is between the selected destination and bind scope. The case gives no evidence that changing DNS, adding an allow rule or restarting an unrelated service is the appropriate correction.

Network Systems Resource Inventory.content:
The core resources cover setup, TCP/UDP, address interpretation, link/routing behavior, listeners, DNS/NSS, reachability, HTTP/TLS, IPv6, policy, packet capture, private exposure and the routed capstone. Optional source packs apply changed ports, prefixes, resolver transport, protocol boundaries and archived evidence to those skills.

Before a live run, inventory the exported role files against its README. Record missing files as an incomplete export. Keep observations and notebook changes beside the source revision. The provided cases use fictional names and reserved example or isolated fixture ranges; they require no personal credentials or public account.

Network Systems Project Ladder.content:
Start with observations requiring an ordinary account: identify the execution context, compare TCP/UDP, read addresses, inspect owned sockets, compare name service and trace local reachability. Continue to HTTP/TLS and IPv6 interpretation. Use the documented disposable Linux environment for live policy, routed topology and capture work, or the supplied records for the same reasoning checkpoints.

The capstone combines both-family paths and two independent faults. The five practice projects below are optional focused revisits, each with its own notebook attempt. Their apparatus is shared with an earlier verified source pack; the requested comparison and saved practice attempt are separate.

Network Systems Checkpoints.content:
| Observation | Supported conclusion | Still open |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A/AAAA answers | Selected resolver returned those records | Connection and application behavior |
| Listener at `127.0.0.1:8080` | Socket is bound in that context | LAN or remote-client reachability |
| HTTP `404` | An HTTP application replied to that request | Whether the intended resource exists |
| HTTP `200` from `owned-denial-control` | A responding backend was reached | Correct intended backend identity |
| No remaining fixture workers | Those workers were reaped | Correct route, policy or application behavior |

Before comparing with the reference, state the narrowest conclusion for each row. The wrong-backend example is resolved by checking configuration, listener, full body and per-run identity, not status alone.

Network Systems Rubric.content:
A complete notebook contains the owned execution boundary, inputs and versions; a prediction; exact commands and unedited observations; the first failed or unmeasured boundary; one controlled change; a retest; cleanup and one remaining limitation.

For example, “IPv4 route lookup fails for `198.18.32.2` with the configured `198.18.32.0/31` route” supports a prefix-coverage diagnosis. “The network is down” exceeds the observation. The recorded IPv6 exchange remains a separate result. A successful program exit supports only the automated controls it actually checked; the notebook explains what those controls establish.

Network Systems Capstone Gate.content:
Before the live capstone, explain both-family prefixes, return paths, resolver transport, listener scope, policy tuples and HTTP identity. Confirm the owned Linux environment supports the namespace and firewall prerequisites in the core README. Keep a fresh output directory for each run.

The supplied-record route uses the [recorded starter, route-only correction, baseline and additional comparisons](/course-assets/network/recorded-capstone-observations-v1.md). Draw the topology, diagnose each family independently, compare the corrected baseline, interpret the bounded packet evidence and review cleanup. Record “supplied records” as the execution route. A walkthrough pauses at the same boundaries; optional archive and practice assignments are additional choices.

Network Systems Allowed Lab Scope.content:
The boundary card names the owned execution environment, issuing account, network namespace, exact destination, protocol and port, permitted observations and cleanup. For a loopback fixture, `127.0.0.1` and `::1` identify the current network context. They do not identify another device.

For the live routed fixture, the program creates an isolated client-router-server topology in a disposable Linux environment. Compare actual namespace identities and its recorded parent before/after checks. The [namespace reference](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/network_namespaces.7.html) explains which network resources belong to that context. A root prompt alone does not demonstrate isolation.

Network Systems Disallowed Work.content:
Course traffic belongs to the owned loopback or isolated fixture endpoints named by its README. Public services, school and employer networks, home routers, personal credentials and third-party packet contents are outside that boundary. Use the fictional names and supplied records instead of substituting a real target.

If an endpoint, route, process owner or namespace differs from the declared fixture, preserve the observation and stop the live attempt. Resolve the boundary with the environment owner before continuing. A supplied-case diagnosis can continue while a live prerequisite is unresolved.

Network Systems Evidence and Remediation.content:
Separate four statements: observation, explanation, correction and verification. In the supplied capstone route-gap case, the client lookup for `198.18.32.2` fails and its configured `198.18.32.0/31` route excludes that address. Correcting the route to the specified `/30` covers the fixture destination. The baseline's route lookup and HTTP exchange provide the comparison.

Preserve IPv6 evidence independently. Keep commands, exit codes, stderr and the actual destination with the explanation. A failed setup command, a successful DNS answer and a successful application response are distinct observations. Finish with the cleanup result and any boundary left unmeasured.

Network Systems Tooling Setup and Recove.content:
Ordinary-account fixtures own their temporary loopback workers and reap them before completion. Privileged fixtures require the disposable Linux environment and check their namespace boundary before changing private routes or policy. Follow the selected README's commands and fresh-output rules.

For a normal run, retain the worker, namespace and parent-state cleanup fields separately from HTTP results. If a live run reports incomplete cleanup, preserve its receipt and use the owned VM's recovery path or snapshot before another attempt. Avoid deleting output folders that contain the first failure. The supplied-record route requires no local service or configuration change.

Network Systems Safety Project: Threat M.content:
Use this supplied situation: an ordinary account will run the TCP/UDP loopback comparison with message `abcdef`. The fixture creates its own temporary ports and workers, records endpoint ownership and reaps those workers.

Write a boundary card covering the execution context, allowed addresses, owned processes, expected observations, stop condition and cleanup. Compare after writing: the targets are this context's `127.0.0.1` sockets, observations include TCP bytes/EOF and separate UDP datagrams/truncation, and unexpected external destinations or process owners stop the live attempt. Record worker reaping and the final PID/socket checks. No router, firewall or public service change is part of this task.

Network Systems Safety Project: Patch an.content:
Use the [recorded route-gap and baseline cases](/course-assets/network/recorded-capstone-observations-v1.md). Write a configuration-correction report with the original prefix, destination, first failure, proposed corrected prefix and expected retest. Keep the original record unchanged.

Self-check: `198.18.32.0/31` covers .0 and .1, excluding the fixture server .2. The specified `198.18.32.0/30` covers .0–.3. Compare the corrected route lookup and actual application identity with the baseline; DNS success alone is insufficient. Include the independently observed IPv6 result and cleanup. This is an explanation using archived records. A fresh live retest uses the owned capstone and a new output folder.

Network Systems Environment and Tooling.content:
The live apparatus runs on Linux with the tools and versions named in each imported README. Ordinary-account labs use loopback sockets and bounded command execution. Routing, firewall and capture fixtures additionally require root and working network/mount namespace capabilities in an owned disposable Linux VM or equivalent isolated lab.

Record `uname -s`, the distribution, account and required tool versions in the terminal that executes the task. A browser editor or remote-editor extension supplies no kernel capability by itself. Missing prerequisites are setup results; the [supplied practice cases](/course-assets/network/network-systems-practice-pack.md) and [recorded capstone packet](/course-assets/network/recorded-capstone-observations-v1.md) remain available for analysis.

Network Systems Prohibited Activity.content:
Keep commands inside the addresses, ports, processes and network contexts declared by the selected fixture. A diagnostic request is still traffic, so substituting a production hostname or an unowned IP changes the scope. An unexplained listener or route is a reason to inspect the boundary before sending traffic.

For a supplied-record exercise, analyze the printed commands and results as data. Documentation addresses and historical output are not instructions to probe a reachable counterpart. Live packet capture is restricted to the fixture's bounded, owned traffic and documented interface.

**Evidence target:** Preserve any mismatched destination, process owner or namespace and the stop condition in the boundary card before a live rerun.

Network Systems Signature Project.content:
The Operations Capstone Studio combines one client, router and server; IPv4 and IPv6; an explicit local resolver; a proxy and loopback backend; least-exposure policy; a bounded capture; two independent faults and cleanup. Its complete core guide specifies the topology and exact runs.

The [recorded failure history and comparison cases](/course-assets/network/recorded-capstone-observations-v1.md) provide a baseline and isolated failures for independent analysis. The route-gap case fails before an IPv4 connection. The wrong-upstream case reaches an HTTP responder with the wrong application identity. Compare both families, the configured endpoint, actual body, denied controls and cleanup. A complete runbook distinguishes those boundaries and the evidence route used.

Network Systems Evidence Rubric.content:
Review the claim against the narrowest supporting record. A route entry shows configuration; a selected route lookup shows a decision for that destination; an HTTP response shows an application exchange. None substitutes for the next boundary.

For the capstone, a strong explanation traces both families, verifies the intended backend identity, retains working denial controls and reconciles the bounded capture with requests. Cleanup must separately show worker reaping, empty remaining namespace state and the recorded parent comparison. Report missing observations as unknown. Leave notebook review open until the written reasoning, corrected comparison and limits are complete.

Network Systems Defensive Lab: Scope and.content:
Use the supplied baseline's cleanup record to plan a reset check before a live capstone. List the owned worker processes, private namespaces, output directory and parent-state comparison. Predict the expected completed cleanup report.

Compare with the [baseline packet](/course-assets/network/recorded-capstone-observations-v1.md): `allWorkersReaped` is true and `remainingNamespaces` is an empty string. The parent before/after snapshots match for the recorded fields. An HTTP success does not imply those results. If a live receipt disagrees, retain it and recover the owned disposable environment before a fresh run. The archived comparison is evidence about that run, not a fresh reset of the current machine.

Network Systems Defensive Lab: Evidence-.content:
Analyze the supplied wrong-upstream case and baseline. Write the observed HTTP status and full body identity, configured backend port, explanation, correction and retest criteria before comparing.

Self-check: port `8088` serves `owned-denial-control`, while the intended loopback backend on `9000` serves `owned-operations-capstone`. The same run token and HTTP `200` can appear at the wrong responder. A completed comparison reconciles configuration, listener, proxy target, body and token within each run, and keeps the public denial-control probes separate. State which remote/public exposure claims remain unmeasured by this private topology.

Include the originating case, observation timestamp, cleanup result and remaining unknown so another reader can distinguish the archived evidence from a proposed fresh retest.

Network Systems Setup Assumptions.content:
The site IDE imports, edits, saves and exports project files. Live network commands execute after extraction in the Linux environment described by that project's README. Python fixtures use the standard library unless their README says otherwise; Bash fixtures require the named Linux tools.

Record exact versions before interpreting differing output. Use an ordinary account for loopback labs; reserve privileged runs for the documented disposable namespace fixtures. macOS and Windows can use the site workspace and supplied-record route. A live Linux VM provides the Linux execution route; a restricted environment can lack required kernel capabilities even when its Python version is suitable.

Network Systems Upgrade Rule.content:
A version difference matters when it changes an option, command result, permission, address selection or response being analyzed. Preserve the exact command, version, exit code and stderr before changing the environment.

For example, an unavailable `ip` command is a missing tool, while a namespace permission error is an environment capability failure. Neither is the intended wrong-prefix incident. Follow the README's setup requirements in the owned environment or use the supplied records. Retain earlier output and compare one changed condition after an authorized environment update; do not relabel setup failure as successful course diagnosis.

Use the Setup and Tooling core project's starter and its README in an ordinary owned Linux account. Record the terminal's `uname -s`, `pwd`, Python version and availability of the listed tools before running the documented command. Keep the imported files together and retain its output.

For a supplied setup check, suppose `uname -s` reports Linux, Python is present, but `command -v dig` returns no path. The name-service live prerequisite is incomplete. Prepare the required DNS tool through the owned environment's normal setup or use the supplied DNS case. Network Systems Version Drift Review.content:
Compare these supplied observations: the README requires Python 3.10 or later; environment A reports Python 3.12 and all required commands; environment B reports Python 3.9; environment C reports Python 3.12 but denies creation of the required network namespace.

Write a decision for each before comparing. A satisfies that version check, but still needs the actual run. B fails the stated Python prerequisite. C passes the Python check but fails the privileged fixture's capability requirement. Preserve each exact result; use the supplied-record route where live prerequisites are absent. A changed output layout alone needs a field-by-field interpretation, while a changed option or permission can change the experiment.

Practice Project: DNS Lookup Explorer.content:
## Compare resolver views

This optional practice revisits the Unit 5 resolver apparatus with a separate notebook attempt. Compare `dual.course.test`, `v4.course.test`, `alias.course.test` and `missing.course.test` at the explicitly selected owned resolver. Predict A, AAAA and alias behavior before each command. Keep the resolver address and port with every result. The ordinary-account live route and all commands appear in the complete guide below.

Record a separate NSS observation with `getent`. The resolver argument supplied to `dig` does not change NSS configuration. A returned A or AAAA record establishes a lookup result, not application reachability. Distinguish an empty answer, NXDOMAIN and a resolver transport error using status, answer and stderr.

### Supplied-case route and self-check

Use the complete [DNS resolution and cache case](/course-assets/network/network-systems-practice-pack.md#dns-resolution-and-cache-case). Preserve the exact requested name, selected server, returned records and NSS view. Diagnose the mismatch before opening the [DNS comparison](/course-assets/network/network-systems-verification-guide.md#dns-resolution-and-cache-key). An NSS result differing from a direct DNS answer establishes different views; the specific cache or override mechanism needs additional evidence.

Keep predictions, commands or case citations, observations, one changed name and the limit of the conclusion in `network-notes.md`. For a walkthrough, pause before each A/AAAA, alias and NSS comparison. Bash programming is optional; equivalent documented observations meet the networking task.

Practice Project: HTTP Request Inspector.content:
## Separate response status, representation and transport

This optional practice uses the Unit 11 owned loopback apparatus in a separate attempt. Predict GET and HEAD behavior before running `python3 main.py`. Compare the supplied normal, missing-path, disallowed-method, unavailable and refused-port observations. Repeat with `--changed --message "Second observation"` and retain both runs. The complete guide below names the ordinary-account Linux prerequisites, response fields and cleanup.

### Supplied comparison

This table is a constructed HTTP case, separate from the live program's generated bodies. The GET representation is the 17 ASCII bytes `{"state":"ready"}`.

| Request | Result | Body transferred | Relevant field |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GET /state | 200 | 17 bytes | Content-Length: 17 |
| HEAD /state | 200 | 0 bytes | Content-Length: 17 |
| GET /missing | 404 | Error representation | HTTP response exists |
| POST /state | 405 | Error representation | Allow: GET, HEAD |
| GET /unavailable | 503 | Error representation | Retry-After: 5 |
| GET to the held non-listening port | Connection refused | No HTTP body | No HTTP response |

Explain why HEAD can describe a representation length while transferring no body. Explain why 404 differs from refusal. Compare after answering: HEAD has the GET metadata without response content; 404 is an application reply; refusal fails before an HTTP response. The status alone does not establish intended responder identity.

Retain exact request, endpoint, status, headers, received bytes, token and worker cleanup in `network-notes.md`. Optional Python analysis can automate the comparison; the required artifact is the explanation. A walkthrough pauses before each changed method, path and endpoint.

Practice Project: Local Client/server To.content:
## Trace message boundaries

This optional practice uses the Unit 1 TCP/UDP fixture with its own saved notebook. Run the ordinary-account loopback commands in the complete guide below. Compare the normal message, a changed message, `--message 'abcdef' --udp-buffer 3` and `--message 'abcdef' --without-newline`. Keep TCP receive bytes and EOF separate from UDP datagram length and truncation.

### Supplied comparison

These are constructed byte observations for reasoning, not claims about the number of reads in a live run:

- TCP reads `6162` then `636465660a` concatenate to seven bytes, `abcdef` followed by newline.
- TCP reads `616263646566` and then EOF contain six bytes with no newline.
- UDP receives an empty datagram, then a separate `616263` datagram with truncation reported for the longer sent message and a three-byte receive buffer.

Identify complete application messages before comparing. The first TCP stream meets the newline rule. The second ends without meeting that rule. The empty UDP datagram is valid; it is not TCP EOF. Truncation means the received UDP payload omits part of that datagram, not that the remaining bytes will arrive in a later receive.

Retain the execution context, endpoints, exact bytes, framing rule and worker cleanup in `network-notes.md`. Loopback does not measure a physical Ethernet link or remote router. Python programming is optional. A walkthrough pauses at each send, receive and application-boundary decision.

Practice Project: Packet Capture Lab Usi.content:
## Explain what the bounded capture selected

This optional practice reuses the Unit 10 capture apparatus in a separate attempt. The live route requires the owned disposable Linux environment and capabilities in the complete guide below. It creates two owned loopback HTTP endpoints; the intended selected-port capture includes the chosen endpoint and excludes the negative-control endpoint. Preserve a first capture before changing `capture-options.sh`. Compare the reversed selected/control ports in a fresh output file.

### Supplied-record route

Use the [bounded packet excerpt](/course-assets/network/network-systems-practice-pack.md#bounded-packet-capture-case) and the baseline `packetRead` in the [recorded capstone packet](/course-assets/network/recorded-capstone-observations-v1.md). The short practice excerpt is constructed; the capstone decoding is an archived routed server-link capture. They have different endpoints and capture positions. Compare each only with its own declared scope.

Mark direction, source/destination, transport ports, handshake evidence, HTTP request line and response identity where present. A SYN alone supplies no complete HTTP exchange; an encrypted payload would not expose the same plaintext. A bounded sample supplies no general throughput estimate. Keep the filter, interface, limits and missing evidence with the interpretation.

Record predictions, raw or supplied excerpt, selected versus control traffic, one changed condition and cleanup in `network-notes.md`. A walkthrough pauses before interpreting each direction. Optional filter scripting extends the task; existing evidence remains available without live capture.

Practice Project: Network Troubleshootin.content:
## Find the first unsupported boundary

This optional practice reuses the Unit 6 reachability apparatus with its own saved notebook. Use only an already owned service and the ordinary-account Linux route in the complete guide below. Record the issuing host, target, numeric port and scheme before invoking the script. A request from the server to itself is a local observation even if it uses another local destination address.

### Supplied case

The complete [diagnostic evidence ladder case](/course-assets/network/network-systems-practice-pack.md#diagnostic-evidence-ladder-case) supplies the process state, loopback listener, local HTTP success, DNS answer, client route and refused remote-address connection. Diagnose it before comparing with the [verification guide](/course-assets/network/network-systems-verification-guide.md#diagnostic-evidence-ladder-key).

A listener at `127.0.0.1:8080` matches the local request but not a request to `192.0.2.10:8080`. That bind-scope mismatch is directly supported. An allow rule does not make a loopback-only listener bind to another address. Keep policy unknown unless supplied observations establish it.

Preserve the raw evidence, first failed or unmeasured boundary, one authorized next observation and its expected outcomes. If a second owned machine is unavailable, label remote behavior unmeasured; retain the supplied case as a separate analysis. Bash programming is optional. A walkthrough pauses after context, lookup, route, socket, transport and application.

Diagnostic Workflow Studio: Core Concept.content:
A diagnostic ladder narrows a claim one boundary at a time. The issuing context determines what `localhost` means. A lookup selects an address; a route selects a path; a listener selects the transport/address/port accepted by a process; an application response adds protocol and identity evidence.

In this studio, a healthy owned service can still be unreachable at a different destination or through the wrong protocol. Preserve the first failure before changing one condition. A refused connection, TLS attempt sent to plaintext HTTP and HTTP application error occur at different boundaries. The core fixture and its complete guide provide the actual local comparison; the optional archive analysis makes no fresh remote measurement.

Diagnostic Workflow Studio: Guided Examp.content:
Use the [supplied diagnostic ladder](/course-assets/network/network-systems-practice-pack.md#diagnostic-evidence-ladder-case) before a live comparison. The process is active, `ss` reports `127.0.0.1:8080`, local HTTP succeeds, DNS returns `192.0.2.10`, a client has a route, and its request to that address is refused.

The successful local request and refused client request use different destination addresses and contexts. The listed bind scope does not accept the non-loopback destination. The supported diagnosis is the listener mismatch; the case does not prove a firewall drop. Propose checking the intended bind address in the owned service configuration, then verifying both the listener and the same client's request after an authorized correction. Keep the original result.

For a live walkthrough, follow the core guide and pause before each context, route, listener and protocol observation. Use fresh output for the changed case. Compare the application response and cleanup independently.

Diagnostic Workflow Studio: Review.content:
Review a notebook by following one exact request. Can another reader identify the issuing host, requested name or literal, selected destination, numeric port and protocol? Does every claimed boundary have its own observation? A route on the service host does not substitute for a route on the client.

For the supplied bind-scope case, retain local success and client refusal together. For the live studio, retain the initial failure and the one-condition correction. Name what could disprove the diagnosis, such as a listener already accepting the exact client destination in the same context. Finish with worker cleanup and the remaining remote or policy uncertainty. Complete the core explanation before choosing a transfer or extension.

Service Exposure Studio: Core Concepts.content:
A proxy adds an application boundary. The client connects to the front listener; the proxy chooses an upstream; the upstream supplies the intended response. A front HTTP `200` can therefore coexist with the wrong backend. Compare the configured upstream and the full response identity, not just the status.

This studio's supplied apparatus observes private owned service paths. Public exposure, internet routing, external DNS and cloud policy are additional boundaries. A private successful exchange supplies no measurement of them. Operations Capstone Studio: Core Concept.content:
The routed capstone combines two address families, a client-router-server path, an explicit resolver, a proxy and loopback backend, least-exposure policy and bounded packet evidence. Each boundary has a separate question: which address was returned, which route selected it, which process listened, what policy applied and which application answered?

The live starter's IPv4 route is `198.18.99.0/30`, which does not cover the server `198.18.32.2`. Its proxy also selects an unavailable loopback upstream on `9001`. The initial IPv4 path fails before an HTTP request; IPv6 can reach the proxy but receives `502`. Correcting only the route leaves `502` in both families. The completed configuration uses `198.18.32.0/30` and the intended backend on `9000`.

Two additional recorded variations test different questions. A `198.18.32.0/31` route excludes .2 despite looking similar to the correct prefix. A proxy choosing `8088` receives HTTP `200` from `owned-denial-control`, while the intended backend identifies itself as `owned-operations-capstone`. Status and token alone do not establish the intended responder.

Use the complete Core Project guide for the owned live route. For independent work without that environment, use the [recorded starter, route-only correction, baseline and additional comparisons](/course-assets/network/recorded-capstone-observations-v1.md). IPv6 Address Categories in Practice.content:
IPv6 is one address family with different address types and scope. The loopback address ::1 remains inside the current node or network namespace. A link-local address in fe80::/10 needs its link/interface context. A global-unicast-shaped address alone establishes neither a selected route nor a working application. The course's 2001:db8::/32 values are documentation examples.

Compare these supplied endpoints: ::1, fe80::1%eth0 and 2001:db8:32::2. Identify the local scope before comparing: the first is loopback; the second includes the link-local zone eth0; the third is a documentation address shaped as global unicast. None of these strings is an application response. For a live fixture, retain its actual route, listener and request separately; for the supplied case, leave unmeasured connectivity unknown.
